Problem 2: need for internet access to do almost anything. It seems to me that a simple bluetooth connection between the fitbit and your phone should suffice to do things like download data, set alarms, etc. But it doesn't; you MUST have an internet connection to set alarms, change time, download data, basically anything. This was very frustrating at first (as my phone didn't have data until a few months ago) but I managed to get past it and work with it. No good if you're going to be out in the woods hiking or camping for a few days, or if you're deployed in the military (both of which apply to me).

By February 2021 it was spending nearly as much time on the charger as it was on my wrist!  Shortly after that the screen started getting horizontal lines in the display.  It quickly got so bad that the display became almost unreadable by March 2021, a month after the warranty expired.  Fortunately I had purchased a protection plan with Asurion and was able to successfully make a claim through them.  I purchased Fitbit branded products with the expectation that they were a name brand and would sell a quality, reliable product.  Now I see their products are of no better quality and reliability than the off-brand trackers that are available at a fourth of the price.  There's no sense in paying a premium price for a device if it's not going to last any longer than the off-brand device.

text:
Like a fool, I assumed that the negative reviews on here were written by people who could not follow instructions to the letter, a nearly lost skill that is often critical in making repairs using adhesives. Was I ever wrong, at least in some cases, I'm sure. I'm thinking the word "Tenacious" was added to the tape backing by some staff member of the manufacturer as an inside joke. I applied a portion of the tape to a properly and thoroughly clean and dry tear in tent material and it barely stuck to the material at all. Not only did I clean the entire area with Isoalcohol, but I was also very careful not to touch the tape adhesive. Now, this may just be a matter that the tent material is polyester with a polyurethane coating and it's possible the adhesive is simply incompatible with it. But if so, the manufacturer surely knows their adhesive will not adhere to this common tent material and should disclose this fact in their product descriptions. Presumably, the product must be working for someone, hence all the many glowing reviews (unless, of course they're all faked).

Everything about this product reeks of maximizing short term profits: chintzy patch portions, tape that won't stick, and a thin plastic case that will shatter into pieces if even minimal pressure is applied to it.

By the way, I did apply the Seam Grip liquid sealer to the backside of the repair area, per the instructions. Still waiting to see if that portion of the repair holds. But even if it works, the tape is still worthless for my purposes.

title: 4 month review—Not comfortable at all
text:
Ordered in October and it is now February. 4 months of use. Sort of.
The exercise-work-bike took a total of 3 days to put together, and had I been doing it alone, I probably never would have gotten it. There is some form of blue “insta-glue” on the pedal screws that made them nearly impossible to screw in. 3 neighborhood kids and teenagers tried their best to help a lady out, but to no avail. Eventually, I hung my head in shame and begged the assistance of male-friend to demonstrate his masculinity and wield tools to get the pedal screwed in.
I am 5’8. That’s 68 inches or about 172cm.
The next issue came when I realized that even at the lowest adjustment, the one recommended for 5’1-5’4 heights, I still struggled to reach the pedals, sitting with my back comfortably against the backrest. If I scooched forward just enough that half my cheeks were off the front of the seat I could reach the pedals, the backrest, and still use the desk for my laptop! But the desk was still a bit high, so I used the tilt-a-table adjustment to relax my wrists and type with perfectly non-ergonomical T-Rex arms.
And now the clunking noise. I can’t stand it. It started off quiet, but after maybe 100 miles of use, it makes a clunking noise from the pedals and no matter how many times I tighten the bolts (almost to stripping them), the seat keeps wobbling and the handle bars offer very little support.

Overall, as a workout bike, it give options that a regular bike doesn’t have—a table.
As for the rest, I am very unhappy with the very little use I got out of it, the lack of structural support for a solid working/workout of cycling, and how fast it has started having issues.

title: Spin = Snake Oil
text: This is only a review of the "Spin" pads.  The Tectal is a great helmet in general, and I have another one.  However, I think the Spin pads are a gimmick.  I bought this one for the extra protection because I like the Tectal so much, but sent it back immediately.  I tried pressing it with varying pressure and moving it on my head in various ways and compared it to my existing helmet.  Both helmets moved on my head identically - in other words they moved the same amount on my skull when pressed against my head -- and this is coming from someone who fits in the Tectal very well head shape wise.  The hair and scalp slip far more than the Spin pads or regular pads for that matter, and I honestly don't see how this would offer any additional rotational protection in a real world impact.  The pads are pretty thin, do not cover much of the scalp, do not cover the back of the head at all, and as I said they don't seem to move any more than the regular pads when pressed against my head in different directions.  Just a way to make more money in my opinion. I would avoid and just get the regular Tectal (which, again is a great helmet and checks the boxes otherwise for safety and comfort).  I'm glad new technologies are being explored, but I think there needs to be more openness about testing and actual data, not just clever youtube videos.  Otherwise the technology is not going to truly progress in the market and people will continue to spend more money without really understanding why with a false sense of security.  In my book Spin and MIPS are both gimmicks and I've tried both.  I'm still on the lookout for new technologies and will continue to explore though -- but not going to pull the trigger again until I see more data and testing, not just videos and slogans.

title: Great concept, poor performance
text:
The concept is extremely well thought out but the performance is just so poor rendering this gadget useless.

The idea is, as you can see, this zero sight system makes a spot on the target. Then after a shot is made, align your rifle back to the exact original spot by using the laser marking you made earlier. Then adjust your firing scope to meet the actual point of impact (calibrating for trajectory rise of course).. and voila.

Sounds incredibly simple and brilliant, right? And it is! But here's the problem.

1. The zero sight is so badly calibrated itself the two lasers do no travel sufficiently parallel so by 100 yrds the spread of two lasers is soooo huge it's more than 6 feet wide. Yes sure if you use the broad side of the barn as your target, then yes, this works. Otherwise there's no way you can simultaneously put two laser markings on a typical 18 inch piece of paper or even 24 inches. Most of your sighting targets are 18 or 24 inches wide with 6 inch circles. Try put two laser dots 6 feet wide on that.

2. Light dispersion. At 10 feet the laser dot is micro millimeter and that is awesome. At 100 yrds... you've got a 2 inch dot. Good luck pin point exactly where your laser making was even if you could put those on a 6 feet wide sheet of paper.

Now you wonder ehh why do you need two parallel dots and why can't 1 dot work? Actually yes in theory you can because it's the same concept on how this laser assisted alignment works. But... but.. one dot you have to be careful to align the rifle back exactly and not slightly rotated. Two dots will be clearly visible that your rifle has rotated slightly. In other words you CAN reposition the laser dot exactly back on where it was but that does not guarantee your rifle is where it was. Try this with any single-dot laser pointer. You can rotate it and the dot will stay put. Now bundle two laser pointers together, and you'll see you have to orient precisely otherwise the two dots won't align. Try and you'll see.

Bottom line is.. yes this product's concept is brilliant but it just performed so poorly at distance.

title: Good solid bike w/power meter, Seat and handle bar a bit weird; perfect bike for skinny giants
text:
Update: ODO = 9832 .Still awaiting pedal straps and post; no call or follow-up from sunny. Tonight I went to pedal, no resistance. I suspect the belt has failed. Though I'm not raving about the quality of this bike, what gets me is the lack of service. 3 months without resolution is unacceptable. I figured sunny would at least have better service than paradigm, but from what I can tell it is identical at best and inferior at worst.
Update: 5 months in still waiting for pedal straps, when I had first major issue. Post attachment for handlebar melted (pic). This product is unsuitable for long intense workouts due to leverage on handlebar. Review has been adjusted from 4 to 3 stars due to first big issue + slow service with inability to send attachments in initial service request. ODO = 7869
Update: Pedal straps broke again 4.5 months ODO = 7403. Bit the bullet and bought a bunch of generics as response time is kinda slow and not worth the downtime when they cost $6/pair. Figure I can use the generics while I wait for the company to mail me new ones. This is typical for these pedal strap types though.
Update: pedal strap broke 2.5 months ODO = 4753
added pedal strap image: this is minor problem, had spare, submitted parts request from MFR will see what happens.
1st review: ODO=2150; 1 month
Got this bike for the power meter. Previous bike seemed to think I have an FTP (1hr power) of 510watts and broke after 17 days of use so I wanted to do some miles before I reviewed. I've been using this for a month now and it reports my FTP as 300 watts which is a bit more realistic and seems to be holding up fine.
The bike is very stable once you get on, but it is a bit difficult to do this in the first place as the seat is very high and may represent a challenge for shorter people and the elderly. I am about 6" and I feel I have to climb on by using the pedals, so I think this could present real problems for shorter people. The seat is adjustable but as it is 39" from floor, it would become uncomfortable for my legs if I went shorter.
Once you're on you have to sit in a hunched over position to reach the HR sensors on the handlebars. This makes sense for aerodynamics in real bikes but I find this position uncomfortable for a stationary cycle. The seat is stable enough so I can balance w/o handlebars, and when I am pushing myself my arms are long enough to reach the front handlebars and this isn't too bad. I think this is a big issue with the bike as it makes it a bit more uncomfortable during long workouts and for those wishing to use the HR mode.
There are a few minor issues. First, I typically cycle at 23-30 MPH yet the bike distance shows that I average 40 miles in 1 hour suggesting that the programmers arent good at math or they or using different units on the same bike (as far as I know there is no metric). Second, if you are looking to quantify you're maximum aneroebic power output this isnt likely to be a good bike for that. This is because the bike stops increasing power output at 120 rpm, and at the maximum mode (16) this is about 348 watts which most people should be able to do for short bursts. This also leads to the problem that at if you want to pedal fast at light loads you will not have an accurate power reading. This is ok for myself as I typically pedal between 90-110 RPM but its frustrating is you want to do wingate HIIT (30s all out) but should be fine for 4x4 HIIT(4 min on/off).
Aside from these quirks I think its a stable well built bike with an accurate power meter which is tough to find in this price range as the last one I bought failed after 17 days.
I think if the MFR could change the handlebar, implement a scan mode, and fix the console bugs without raising the price this would be an amazing bike. However, even with its quirks it remains a pretty good bike for the money. I will update this review after a few thousand miles.
Likes:
Stable
quiet (mostly)
Power meter
ybeki pedals 0.75"
packaged absurdly well (even has metal tubes to protect body of bike during shipping)
calories burned/mile is modulated by resistance setting (most bikes under 300 don't have this)
programs (I don;t really use these but they are available)
Body fat and power clamp mode
easy assembly
Dislikes:
Manual isnt very clear(how to display power/rpm by pressing mode button) paragraphs need indentation
Handlebar is very uncomfortable and not adjustable when using hr sensor, has user in hunched over aerodynamic position which is pretty weird for a stationary bike
Handlebar squeaks during intense workouts and needs to be tightened every now and again (I think its just so long you have alot of leverage where the grip is)
Seating height is very high and you have to "climb on" which could be difficult for short people
Bike is designed for very tall people which is kinda inconsistent with its 240lb weight limit (tall people tend to be heavier)
when system switches it can make unsettling clunks and feel a bit gritty
requires ac adapter
workout info lost when it goes to sleep after 4 minutes so if you get interrupted you have to write down your stats
Display distance is inconsistent with speed (how do I accomplish 40 miles per hour when I typically only cycle at 20-30MPH)

title: Read this if you’re trying to decide between a Gear Fit 2 and Fitbit Charge 2!
text:
After a ton of research about Fitbit products, I purchased the Fitbit Charge 2 as an upgrade to my Fitbit One. I had to return/exchange the Charge 2 as the step count was wildly inaccurate. Fitbit advised that this was a defect and provided a new device promptly. However, the new device had the exact same issue. Both Charge 2’s have been returned.
I then broadened my research beyond Fitbit products and was stunned to learn at how much more I could get for my money if I opened my mind beyond the popular Fitbit product line. I ended up purchasing a Samsung Gear Fit 2 and am very happy I did.

I’ve used the Charge 2 and Gear Fit 2 each for at least a month, and here’s my take on how they compare -

*Accuracy:
This is the main deciding factor for me. The Charge 2 was wildly inaccurate (keep in mind, I received 2 devices from Fitbit as noted above – both with the same issue). It consistently missed over 1,500 steps a day and counted steps while I slept somehow. My Fitbit One didn’t have this issue. Fitbit customer support suggested I place the Charge 2 in my pocket for improved accuracy, which completely negated the purpose of upgrading from the One to the Charge 2.
The Gear Fit 2 is pretty spot on. I say ‘pretty’ because the only time it’s slightly off is when I walk in place, and that’s OK with me because I’m cheating anyway… It also accurately counts repetitions when using the different Exercise features (lunges, crunches, squats), which is really cool and helpful.

*Features/Functionality:
The Gear Fit 2 is the clear winner here. The biggest reason is that if you’re looking to keep track of how you’re doing with your fitness goals, even if you’re just casually trying to improve your fitness level, it really makes it easy by improving awareness. For example, when viewing any item such as floors or steps, not only do you see today’s activity, but you also see how you did for the rest of the week at a glance. Tapping on those screens displays the detail by day. You can get more detail on the exercise done (map, etc) if you want to from these screens as well. There's really not much of a need to use the app with the Gear Fit 2.
The Charge 2 will display this detail within the app only, as far as I know.
I tried the guided breathing feature on the Charge 2 a few times and didn’t really find any value in it. To each their own.
The Gear Fit 2 has built in GPS (no phone required!), so once you’re done with your run/walk/hike, you can view your route, distance, average MPH and much more, right on your wrist.
MyFitnessPal works really well with the Gear Fit 2 so you can quick add foods directly from your wrist and log water intake with a couple of taps.
With the Gear Fit 2, I can play music from my phone or store music directly on the device. I can view/dismiss Alarms directly from the screen. I love the ability to set a button to quick launch a feature. I use it to quick launch an Exercise, so all I have to do is press the button, and I’m off! On the Charge 2, you’d have to tap thru the screens, then press/hold to launch the Exercise - this was kind of a PITA for me and I usually forgot to do it before I set off on my adventure.
One thing that I really love, which may not be a big deal to many other folks, is the ability to quickly set the Gear Fit 2 to ‘do not disturb’ mode. This means that the all alerts are muted and device won’t wake when you move your wrist. It’s great to use when sleeping so you don’t light up the room at night!

*Comfort:
The Gear Fit 2 blows the Charge 2 away here. You can tell by the photo that the Charge 2 doesn’t sit flush to the wrist area, largely due to the lumpy bottom and straight face. This made me abundantly aware that I had something on my wrist every second of every day that I wore it. It was downright painful to wear while sleeping if I put any pressure on that wrist (if I slept on that side). *Customization: It’s kind of a split here, but I’d have to say that overall, the Gear Fit 2 wins.
The Charge 2 has the advantage over the Gear Fit 2 in the band category since there are so many different bands to choose from. I’m really not sure why there aren’t more available for the Gear Fit 2, but I will say that I’m happy with the options that I’ve found. There’s a great magnetic Milanese one out there that I love. The Gear Fit 2 wins over the Charge 2 with respect to the customization features available directly within the device. *Battery Life:
It’s a draw. Some complain that the Gear Fit 2 has too short of a battery life, but that’s not been a problem for me. I set the screen brightness to 3, which is still plenty bright, and use a clock face with a mostly black background. I didn’t really find many features within the Charge 2 that would encourage me to push to meet my fitness goals. Although I did like how the Charge 2 had automatic reminders to move 10 minutes before each hour.

For me, the clear winner is the Gear Fit 2. I absolutely love it.

Fitbit is basic, simple and stripped down versus the Gear Fit 2, which is feature loaded and very customizable. It can be overwhelming to some that just want a device that comes out of the box with no other options.
Personally, I love the mere fact that the Gear Fit 2 is accurate in addition to the additional features, having the ability to customize and the ease of use that the Gear Fit 2 has versus the Charge 2.

title: Horrible inaccuracies (off by up to 59 BPM heart rate)make it worthless
text:
I should start by saying I own the Charge 2, but after 6 months I came to trash it with a lousy review and found that it had been superceded by the charge 3.

Looking at the bad reviews for the 3, I feel like I should do my bit to warn off anyone curious to try it.

There are three good things about the Fitbit.

1. The step tracker is pretty accurate.

2. The app is well designed and has lots of features, although the diet tracker is pretty substandard (you'd do better with MyFitnessPal).

3 the sleep tracker was interesting and seems fairly accurate when it comes to tracking how long you actually slept. However, there's no way to tell if the information about REM and deep sleep states are accurate in any way. I'm inclined to suspect not because both the heart rate monitor and the oximetry tool both work by shining light through the skin to illuminate blood vessels.

The bad.

I recently bought a chest strap heart monitor because i was getting such divergent readings from fitbit heart rate monitor.

Putting the results side by side was very instructive and confirmed my own self administered pulse counts that I had begun to so when I could no longer believe what my Fitbit was telling me.

There were times when my chest strap had my heart rate at 178 but my Fitbit was telling me my heart rate was at 119. And that my friends, is dangerously inaccurate.

Fitbit will tell you to try various positioning tricks and these will improve your accuracy.. a bit. It was still way off, plus now I have to worry about whether the watchchas moved at all during a strenuous workout or a run and you know what? Screw that.

Ask Fitbit for a refund and they will refer you to Amazon. I think they should take responsibility for their weaksauce product, sack up, and refund users who are deeply unhappy with their purchase.

What you need to think about before you buy is that if one sensor or function is so wildly off, how can you trust any of them unless you are able to double check the accuracy for yourself (like with the pace tracker)?

This effectively makes most of the rest of it next to useless. Recommend you avoid.

title: Smelly, sticky latex rubber - too short for pull-ups.
text:
I have the LifeLines and BodyLastics band systems. These systems use smooth rubber bands that attach to hand grips, leg grips, and pull-up assist pieces. Rubberbanditz have the feel of large rubber bands. Personally, I prefer the smooth rubber of LifeLines/BodyLastics with their handle pieces so that your hands don't smell like rubber for hours after working out as they do with Rubberbanditz. If you have a latex allergy, stay away.

The benefits of the loops are you can fit more bands in your bag and it's easier to switch resistance. However, as pull-up assist bands for an Iron Gym bar ~6.5 feet high, the bands are too short and the bottom loop hangs about 3.5 feet above the floor so they are too high to step into for anyone below 6 foot. I hoped that unlike the LifeLines pull-up revolution, there would be no plastic parts that will snag on your clothing as you move up or down, but this sticky, unfinished rubber grabs your skin, clothes, and leg hair and is generally uncomfortable for pullups.

I kind of expected them to be cheaper for what they are. How much more costly is a slightly thicker rubber band to make?

I really wanted to like these, but for my purposes they were a waste of money.

Price - I paid less than $10. The solar heating of the water works well.

We never used the product as a true "shower" - i.e. we did not hang the bag from a tree etc. Keep in mind 5 gallons of water weighs over 40 pounds.... so you have to be able to hang it and have something to be able to hold the weight. Since we had such challenges with the thing - we opted to try to not move it very often and just keep it on our camping tub on the picnic table.

title: Be prepared.
text: Let me recount this while the humiliation is fresh so I don't miss any details. My hydration belt came in on Thursday and I was super excited to try it out today, as I planned a 6 mile run at 2:00 pm when my phone informed me that it felt like 107 degrees. So I wash the bottles, adjust the belt, grab my sunglasses and head out. I make it about a quarter mile before I have to stop and adjust the belt because it's just really bouncy. I make it as tight as it will go, and it's still bouncy. I think about going home and dropping it off because it's bothering me, but I don't. I get about a mile into my run and it's really bothering me so I decide if I drink some and squirt some on my head it will be lighter and less bouncy. Wrong. Still bouncy, but now my butt feels cold. I start to wonder are the bottles leaking? Oh no! Are they getting water on my new phone? So I stop and check the bottles. Not leaking. Great, this fanny pack is just making me have a lot of butt sweat because the neoprene phone pouch is hot. By now I'm out of my subdivision and on a fairly busy road. I'm getting honked at. (I am wearing oversized race shirts and medium length running shorts, not much to honk at.) My butt is still really cool. So I reach back to see exactly how sweaty I am. I AM NOT SWEATY! The bouncing of the belt has pushed my shorts down, but also held my shirt in place... it is laundry day... MY LAST PAIR OF UNDERWEAR IS FULLY EXPOSED!!!! I quickly rip the hydration belt off and pull up my shorts. I run home the fastest course back half wondering if I should just ditch the belt on the side of the road, but I can't. My dad has rubbed off on me and I cannot waste it! I try wearing it like a messenger bag, it strangles me. I carry it until I make it inside the walls of my subdivision, then make it as big as the straps will go, put it across my back, under my arms, over my shoulders, and snap it behind my neck so it's like a back pack. I jog home and drop it on the front porch and I finish my 6 mile run hot, tired, sweaty, and thirsty, but FULLY clothed.

title: There are better options for water filtration
text:
Just purchased several of these bottles for a family trip to the Amazon and Pantanal regions of Brazil. Bottom Line: save your money. If you truly need a portable water filtration/purification system (which I found out I didn't in Brazil as there was bottled water available everywhere) this is probably not the system for you. First it is very heavy. The mechanism is clumsy requiring you to unscrew the bottle, add water, rescrew the now full bottle, pump it a bit, open the valve with your teeth, quickly catch the water that spurts out, close the valve with your teeth (making it nearly impossible not to contaminate the valve), pump it some more, repeat the process for a little more water.
There are other filters out there, especially those that can be placed in-line on a Camelbak system that are lighter and much more effective and efficient.
